cve_candidates.description: Werkzeug debugger PIN bypass leading to RCE via crafted __debugger__ requests; affects versions < 3.0.3. If debug mode is active on the Flask dev server (confirmed likely by /debug 200 OK response), an attacker can bypass the PIN mechanism and gain access to the interactive Python console, enabling arbitrary code execution on the host.
Werkzeug denial-of-service via large multipart body parsing; primarily affects versions < 2.3.0. Low applicability to 2.3.7 but noted for completeness.

PyYAML yaml.load() without explicit Loader= argument allows Python object deserialization RCE. OSINT confirmed server-side YAML parsing at /api/parse-config (POST endpoint, Content-Type: text/yaml per client source). If yaml.load() is used unsafely, a crafted YAML payload (!!python/object/apply:os.system) yields remote code execution.
Additional PyYAML unsafe deserialization RCE vector, similar to CVE-2017-18342. Arbitrary code execution via malicious YAML document submitted to the /api/parse-config endpoint.

attack_surface_summary: The target is a minimal Linux container (10.10.20.30) exposing a single service: a Flask/Werkzeug 2.3.7 development web server on port 5000. The attack surface is narrow in breadth but critically deep in severity. Three web paths are confirmed: root (/), a live debug endpoint (/debug, HTTP 200), and a YAML-parsing API (/api/parse-config, HTTP 405 on GET — expects POST). The presence of /debug returning 200 OK strongly suggests Werkzeug debug mode is active, which — combined with CVE-2024-34069 — provides a direct path to interactive Python console RCE if the PIN can be bypassed using system files (/proc/self/cgroup, /sys/class/net/*/address, /sys/kernel/boot_id). Independently, the /api/parse-config endpoint accepts raw YAML (confirmed via OSINT of the client source code), and if PyYAML is used without a safe Loader, a single crafted POST body achieves unauthenticated RCE via object deserialization (CVE-2017-18342 / CVE-2020-1747). The origin host was fully concealed behind Cloudflare on the public domain but was recovered from a staging .env file inadvertently committed to the public GitHub repository and deleted three days later — remaining permanently accessible in git history. No credentials, breach records, or dark-web exposure were identified at the surface tier for this domain.
